newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Britain, Sinn Fein, said to discuss IRA truce - report.
newsitem.headline: Britain, Sinn Fein, said to discuss IRA truce - report.

text.p: Britain is negotiating with Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams to secure a new ceasefire from his IRA guerrrilla allies before Christmas, Dublin's Sunday Tribune newspaper said.

By its account, John Hume, leader of Northern Ireland's moderate Irish nationalists SDLP group, has acted as a go-between in talks over the past week with British government officials, the report said.

A spokesman for British Prime Minister John Major said he had no knowledge of any such negotiations. Britain has shunned any official contact with Sinn Fein, which seeks an end to British rule of Northern Ireland, since the IRA ended a truce in February.
Neither Adams nor Hume, the main representatives of Irish nationalism in the British province, were immediately available for comment on the report.
The Sunday Tribune said the negotiations "may turn out to be the most serious effort to restore the Irish Republican Army cessation since it broke down in February."

The Irish government, Britain's partner in the quest for a lasting Northern Ireland settlement, was aware of the contacts but was playing a secondary role, the newspaper said. The Dublin government has also banned meetings with Sinn Fein until the IRA truce is renewed.
The Sunday Tribune report coincided with media stories of a secret weekend meeting by the IRA's top decision-taking body, the General Army Convention, which has only met twice in the past 27 years.

Irish officials said they were unaware of any such meeting by the IRA, membership of which is illegal in both Ireland and Britain. Police and politicians also cast doubts on reports of such a meeting.

The British and Irish governments say that Sinn Fein cannot take part in Belfast peace talks being attended by every other political party in the province until the IRA renews the ceasefire it ended in February with bomb attacks in Britain, Germany and Northern Ireland itself.

It killed one soldier and injured 20 when it detonated two powerful car bombs at Britain's Northern Ireland army base in Lisburn, outside Belfast, on October 7, its first attack in the province for more than two years.

The Sunday Tribune said the British government and Adams were trying to draft a statement setting out the terms under which an IRA ceasefire would allow Sinn Fein to take part in the peace talks, which are being chaired by former U.S. Senator George Mitchell.
It said Sinn Fein wanted immediate entry into the Belfast talks as soon as a ceasefire was declared but Britain wanted a three-month delay to make sure that the truce was lasting.

The report seemed certain to anger Northern Ireland's Protestant Unionist parties, which want the province to stay British and suspect the British government of trying to ease Sinn Fein's path to the peace talks to make sure that all sides in the 27-year conflict are represented.
The IRA declared a truce in August 1994 but went back to war in February accusing the British government of trying to use the talks to force the guerrillas to surrender their stockpiles of arms.
Britain said it did not want the issue of arms "decommissioning" to hold up the talks but the IRA said in a statement that any attempt to seek the surrender of its weapons was ludicrous.
Unionists and the British government say that no political party can take part in the negotiations while it has armed supporters who could seek to wreck any agreement they disliked.
